items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a graph showing how river discharge changes over a short period in response to a rainfall event”.
items.answer: Storm hydrograph
items.markingKey: Storm hydrograph: a graph showing how river discharge changes over a short period in response to a rainfall event. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the rising limb of a storm hydrograph is usually steeper than the falling limb.
items.answer: Water reaches the river quickly by overland flow and channel precipitation, but afterwards slower throughflow and groundwater flow continue to drain into the river for a long time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark quick inputs; 1 mark slow drainage [2]

items.stem: Explain why baseflow rises slightly during and after a storm.
items.answer: Some rainfall percolates to groundwater and raises the water table, increasing groundwater flow to the river a little later.
items.markingKey: 1 mark recharge; 1 mark delayed release [2]

items.stem: “The shape of a storm hydrograph depends more on the characteristics of the storm than on the characteristics of the drainage basin.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to rainfall intensity and antecedent conditions.
items.answer: For: Rainfall intensity, duration and total; antecedent rainfall; snowmelt or rain on frozen ground; storm movement down the basin; e.g. the 2021 Ahr valley (Germany) flood after over 100 mm in 24 hours. Against: Basin size and shape, slope, rock permeability, soils, drainage density and land use (urbanisation, forest cover) set lag time and peak; the same storm gives very different hydrographs in permeable chalk and impermeable clay basins. Conclusion: Storm characteristics trigger each event and explain differences between storms in one basin, but basin characteristics explain the consistent differences between basins.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “storm hydrograph”?
options: The maximum discharge reached during a storm event.
The part of a storm hydrograph showing increasing discharge after rainfall begins.
The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge.
A graph showing how river discharge changes over a short period in response to a rainfall event.
items.answer: A graph showing how river discharge changes over a short period in response to a rainfall event.
items.markingKey: Storm hydrograph: a graph showing how river discharge changes over a short period in response to a rainfall event. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “A short lag time means that there is a lower risk of flooding.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. A short lag time means water arrives quickly and the peak is high, which increases flood risk.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe the characteristics of a “flashy” hydrograph.
items.answer: Short lag time, steep rising limb, high peak discharge and a quick return to baseflow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per feature [3]

items.stem: Explain why river discharge may remain high even after rainfall has stopped.
items.answer: Water stored in soil, on the surface and in channels upstream continues to arrive at the gauging station; travel time from distant parts of the basin; throughflow and groundwater flow are slow.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Baseflow is the water that flows over the surface during a storm.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why river discharge may remain high even after rainfall has stopped.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Baseflow is groundwater-fed flow; surface flow during a storm is part of stormflow. (b) Water stored in soil, on the surface and in channels upstream continues to arrive at the gauging station; travel time from distant parts of the basin; throughflow and groundwater flow are slow.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain how urbanisation affects the shape of a storm hydrograph.
items.answer: Impermeable surfaces reduce infiltration; drains and gutters carry water rapidly to rivers; less vegetation so less interception and evapotranspiration; channelised rivers; result: shorter lag, higher and steeper peak.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point [4]

items.stem: Explain how rock type influences the storm hydrograph.
items.answer: Permeable rocks (chalk, sandstone) allow percolation, so more water travels slowly as groundwater: long lag, low peak; impermeable rocks (granite, clay) cause overland flow: short lag, high peak.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each rock type with effect [3]

items.answer: Basin Y: higher peak reached quickly, giving less warning and more chance of exceeding bankfull discharge.

items.stem: Assess the view that human activities now have more influence on flood hydrographs than physical factors.
items.answer: For: Urbanisation (e.g. Houston, where impervious surfaces made the 2017 Hurricane Harvey floods worse); deforestation in the Himalaya; field drainage; channelisation speeding flows downstream. Against: Physical factors such as storm intensity, basin size, rock and slope still control most hydrographs; extreme rainfall can overwhelm any land use; reservoirs and afforestation can reduce peaks, so human influence is not only negative. Conclusion: In urban and heavily modified basins human activity dominates, but in most basins physical factors remain more important, and human influence can lower as well as raise flood peaks.

items.answer: Not correct. Water has further to travel in large basins, so lag times are usually longer.

items.stem: Explain why a basin’s shape affects peak discharge.
items.answer: In a circular basin water from all parts has a similar distance to travel and arrives at the outlet at about the same time, giving a high peak; in an elongated basin arrival is spread out.

items.stem: Explain why large rivers such as the Mississippi often have complex regimes.
items.answer: Tributaries drain areas with different climates and relief (snowmelt from the Rockies, spring rain in the Ohio basin), so peaks arrive at different times.
items.markingKey: 1 mark tributaries; 1 mark different climates; 1 mark example [3]

items.stem: Table 2.3 shows mean monthly discharge (m³/s) of River N. Jan 5, Feb 5, Mar 6, Apr 13, May 32, Jun 48, Jul 50, Aug 38, Sep 21, Oct 11, Nov 7, Dec 6. Calculate the mean monthly discharge.
Outline the evidence that supports, and the evidence that challenges, the view that climate is the only important influence on river regimes.
items.answer: For: Seasonal rainfall, snowmelt and evapotranspiration explain most regimes (monsoonal Ganges, nival Rhône, Mediterranean rivers). Against: Basin geology (aquifers smooth regimes), lakes and wetlands, basin size and tributaries, and human activity (dams such as Aswan, irrigation abstraction from the Colorado) also matter. Conclusion: Climate is the dominant control, but geology, basin size and especially human regulation strongly modify regimes.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Reservoirs can reduce flood peaks downstream.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They store storm water and release it slowly, as on the Yangtze below the Three Gorges Dam.

items.stem: Explain how afforestation could change the hydrograph of an upland basin.
items.answer: More interception and evapotranspiration; roots and litter increase infiltration; less overland flow; longer lag, lower peak; but drainage ditches during planting can initially increase runoff.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Fig. 2.2 shows storm hydrographs for two neighbouring basins after the same storm. Basin X (mainly forest on sandstone) had a lag time of 20 hours and a peak of 35 m³/s. items.answer: Sustainable urban drainage (permeable paving, green roofs, retention ponds); planting trees upstream; flood storage areas; channel improvements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Two basins of similar size received the same 45 mm storm. In Basin X, on forested sandstone, discharge peaked 20 hours after peak rainfall at 35 m³/s; in Basin Y, a partly urbanised clay basin, discharge peaked after 6 hours at 95 m³/s. (a) Suggest which basin would be more likely to flood and why. (b) Suggest two ways the flood risk in Basin Y could be reduced.
items.answer: (a) Basin Y: higher peak reached quickly, giving less warning and more chance of exceeding bankfull discharge. (b) Sustainable urban drainage (permeable paving, green roofs, retention ponds); planting trees upstream; flood storage areas; channel improvements.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark choice; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “river regime”?
options: A regime with one period of high discharge and one of low discharge each year.
A regime dominated by snowmelt, with peak discharge in spring or early summer.
The annual variation in the discharge of a river.
A regime with more than one peak in the year, often in large rivers fed by tributaries with different climates.
items.answer: The annual variation in the discharge of a river.
items.markingKey: River regime: the annual variation in the discharge of a river. [1]

items.stem: Explain how human activity can modify a river regime.
items.answer: Dams and reservoirs even out flows; abstraction for irrigation lowers flows; urbanisation adds quickflow; inter-basin transfers add water.

items.stem: “Climate is the only important influence on river regimes.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to snowmelt, dams and abstraction.
items.answer: For: Seasonal rainfall, snowmelt and evapotranspiration explain most regimes (monsoonal Ganges, nival Rhône, Mediterranean rivers). Against: Basin geology (aquifers smooth regimes), lakes and wetlands, basin size and tributaries, and human activity (dams such as Aswan, irrigation abstraction from the Colorado) also matter. Conclusion: Climate is the dominant control, but geology, basin size and especially human regulation strongly modify regimes.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why river discharge may remain high even after rainfall has stopped. (b) A student writes: “A short lag time means that there is a lower risk of flooding.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Water stored in soil, on the surface and in channels upstream continues to arrive at the gauging station; travel time from distant parts of the basin; throughflow and groundwater flow are slow. (b) Not correct. A short lag time means water arrives quickly and the peak is high, which increases flood risk.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Baseflow is the water that flows over the surface during a storm.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why river discharge may remain high even after rainfall has stopped.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Baseflow is groundwater-fed flow; surface flow during a storm is part of stormflow. (b) Water stored in soil, on the surface and in channels upstream continues to arrive at the gauging station; travel time from distant parts of the basin; throughflow and groundwater flow are slow.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why river discharge may remain high even after rainfall has stopped. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Two storms of the same size can produce different hydrographs in the same basin.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Water stored in soil, on the surface and in channels upstream continues to arrive at the gauging station; travel time from distant parts of the basin; throughflow and groundwater flow are slow. (b) Correct. Antecedent soil moisture, frozen ground, storm path and intensity all differ between events.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Steep slopes reduce the amount of infiltration.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Water moves downslope more quickly, so there is less time to infiltrate and more overland flow.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how rock type influences the storm hydrograph. (b) Explain how afforestation could change the hydrograph of an upland basin.
items.answer: (a) Permeable rocks (chalk, sandstone) allow percolation, so more water travels slowly as groundwater: long lag, low peak; impermeable rocks (granite, clay) cause overland flow: short lag, high peak. (b) More interception and evapotranspiration; roots and litter increase infiltration; less overland flow; longer lag, lower peak; but drainage ditches during planting can initially increase runoff.
